paragraphs.source_en: We usually do not think of Mehmed II when we think of the Renaissance. What comes to mind instead are the Medici family ruling Florence; Dante Alighieri’s Divine Comedy (1321); Filippo Brunelleschi’s cathedral dome in Florence (1436); Leonardo da Vinci’s paintings The Last Supper (1495-1498) and Mona Lisa (1503-1506); Niccolo Machiavelli’s The Prince (1513); and Michelangelo’s sculpture of David (1501-1504) and Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508-1512) in the Vatican. Generally understood as the revival of classical culture and learning in fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Western Europe, the Renaissance is not thought to have encompassed the Ottomans and their empire. If we think of the Ottomans and the Renaissance at all, it is with a negative association based on two myths.

paragraphs.source_en: In the twelfth, thirteenth, and fourteenth centuries, this humanistic worldview and knowledge was then transmitted to Christian Europe through Islamic Spain and Sicily when it was translated from Arabic into Hebrew and Latin. The Divine Comedy’s section entitled ‘Inferno’ demonstrates that Dante was familiar with Islamic narratives of Muhammad’s ascent to paradise and used it as a framing device for this work. Thus, the European Renaissance has its roots in Islamic Spain and the Arab world.
